zones.label: Product Stage (A1 to A3)
zones.summary: The carbon of making the materials: digging, hauling raw materials, and manufacturing them in a factory.
facts: Modules A1 to A3 cover raw material extraction, transport to the factory, and manufacturing (RICS, following EN 15978).
Ending the count here is called cradle to gate, and it is the scope a typical product EPD reports (Chapter 20).
Cement making releases carbon dioxide from the limestone itself, and steel and aluminum need high-temperature process heat (Chapter 20).
RICS defines upfront carbon as everything emitted up to practical completion, which includes this stage.

zones.label: Transport and Construction (A4 to A5)
zones.summary: The carbon of getting products to the site and building with them, including the waste the jobsite makes.
facts: A4 covers transporting products to the site; A5 covers construction processes, including wastage, up to completion (RICS).
Transport is often a small share of a product's embodied carbon compared with manufacturing, so check the EPD before assuming local means low-carbon (Chapter 20).
Cutting waste on the jobsite lowers A5 and also lowers the A1 to A3 carbon of material that never had to be bought.
After A5 the building is complete, and every module so far has happened before the first occupant moves in.

zones.label: Use Stage: Upkeep and Replacement (B1 to B5)
zones.summary: The carbon of keeping the building going: repainting, repairs, replacing worn parts, and later refurbishment.
facts: B1 is direct emissions from products in use, such as refrigerant leakage; B2 to B4 are maintenance, repair, and replacement; B5 is planned refurbishment (RICS).
These modules are material-related, so they count as embodied carbon even though they happen while the building is occupied (RICS).
A short-lived finish or window that is replaced several times can add more embodied carbon than a long-lived one that costs more upfront.
Durable materials and good maintenance are carbon strategies because they avoid repeating A1 to A5 (Chapter 21).

zones.label: Use Stage: Energy and Water (B6 to B7)
zones.summary: The carbon of running the building: the energy and water it uses every year, read off the meters.
facts: B6 covers the energy a building uses in operation and B7 covers its water use over the in-use stage (RICS).
RICS always classes B6 and B7 as operational carbon, and the rest of the use stage as embodied.
Operating carbon repeats every year and depends on the electric grid, which may get cleaner over the building's life (Chapter 20).
Efficient envelopes and equipment shrink this stage, which is what raises the share of materials in the total (Chapter 19).

zones.label: End of Life (C1 to C4)
zones.summary: The carbon of taking the building apart: demolition, hauling debris, sorting and processing waste, and disposal.
facts: C1 to C4 cover deconstruction or demolition, waste transport, waste processing, and disposal (RICS, following EN 15978).
Ending the count here is called cradle to grave.
Careful deconstruction keeps materials in better shape for reuse than demolition that mixes everything together (Chapter 21).
How much of this debris is reused instead of landfilled is reported separately, in Module D.

zones.label: Module D: Beyond the Boundary
zones.summary: The potential benefits of reuse and recycling after the building's life, drawn as a loop from the end back to the start.
facts: Module D reports potential benefits and loads beyond the system boundary from reuse, recycling, and energy recovery (RICS).
RICS reports Module D separately from the whole-life-carbon total, so a recycling credit never hides the emissions of A to C.
Including reuse makes the boundary cradle to cradle; a recycled beam can displace the need to make a new one (Chapter 20).
The benefit is only potential: it depends on the material being recovered, kept clean, and actually used again.

zones.label: Embodied Carbon: Making, Building, and Upkeep
zones.summary: Embodied carbon spans the product and construction stages and the upkeep modules of the use stage.
facts: Embodied carbon is everything material-related: modules A1 to A5, B1 to B5, and C1 to C4 (RICS, whole life carbon assessment).
RICS's 2023 standard also lists a pre-construction module A0, assumed to be zero for buildings, so this poster starts at A1.
Embodied carbon is not one block at the start: the use-stage upkeep modules repeat across the building's life.
The left-hand bracket covers A1 to A5 and B1 to B5; the end-of-life modules belong to embodied carbon too, at the far right.

zones.label: Operational Carbon: Energy and Water
zones.summary: Operational carbon is only modules B6 and B7: the energy and water the building uses while occupied.
facts: RICS defines operational carbon as modules B6 and B7, the impacts from energy and water use.
A cleaner electric grid shrinks this bracket but does nothing about the embodied carbon already emitted in the other modules (Chapter 20).
Whole life carbon adds embodied and operational carbon together, so improving one at the cost of the other can backfire (RICS).
Chapter 19 covers how to reduce this bracket; Chapter 20 covers the rest.

zones.label: Embodied Carbon: End of Life
zones.summary: The end-of-life modules also count as embodied carbon, because the emissions come from handling materials.
facts: C1 to C4 are part of embodied carbon in the RICS definition, alongside A and the upkeep modules of B (RICS).
The poster shows two embodied brackets with a gap between them because the operational modules sit in the middle of the building's life.
Chapter 20's illustrative ledger gives end of life far less than the product stage (20 versus 330 tonnes), so it is easy to overlook, but it is still counted.
Design for disassembly can lower this bracket and increase the Module D benefit at the same time (Chapter 21).

quiz.question: A quarry blasts limestone and a kiln fires it into cement. Which region of the life cycle includes those emissions?
quiz.explanation: Raw material extraction, transport to the factory, and manufacturing make up the product stage, also called cradle to gate.

quiz.question: A concrete truck delivers a pour and a crane lifts steel into place. Which region counts those emissions, plus the waste the crew throws away?
quiz.explanation: Transporting products to the site and the construction process, including wastage, are counted together up to completion.

quiz.question: Ten years after opening, the owner repaints, repairs a leak, and replaces a worn-out window. Which region captures the carbon of that work?
quiz.explanation: Maintenance, repair, replacement, and refurbishment are material-related, so they count as embodied carbon in the use stage.

quiz.question: A meter records the electricity and the water a building uses every month. Which region does that reading feed?
quiz.explanation: Energy and water use in operation are counted in the final two use-stage modules and are always classed as operational carbon.

quiz.question: A wrecking crew demolishes a building and trucks the debris to a sorting yard and then to a landfill. Which region counts that?
quiz.explanation: Demolition, waste transport, waste processing, and disposal make up the end-of-life stage, the end of a cradle-to-grave count.

quiz.question: A beam is pulled out of a demolished building, cleaned, and used in a new project. Which region reports that potential benefit, separately from the main total?
quiz.explanation: Reuse, recycling, and energy recovery are reported outside the system boundary, which turns cradle to grave into cradle to cradle.

quiz.question: Which bracket covers all material-related emissions during manufacture, construction, and upkeep, even though some happen while the building is occupied?
quiz.explanation: Embodied carbon includes the product, construction, and upkeep modules, so the use-stage maintenance modules belong here.

quiz.question: Which bracket is limited to just two modules, the building's energy and water use, and never includes materials?
quiz.explanation: Operational carbon is only the energy and water modules; everything material-related is embodied.

quiz.question: An engineer says that demolition and disposal emissions count as embodied carbon even though they come at the very end. Which region confirms it?
quiz.explanation: In the RICS definition, the end-of-life modules are embodied carbon alongside the product, construction, and upkeep modules.

quiz.question: A team chooses a window that lasts twice as long, so it is replaced fewer times. Which stage's carbon does that choice reduce?
quiz.explanation: Replacement is counted in the use stage, so a longer-lived component avoids repeating the product and construction emissions.
